newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa maize buyers first U.S. shipment arrives.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa maize buyers first U.S. shipment arrives.

text.p: A 57,500 tonne shipment of U.S. maize will arrive in Cape Town harbour on Sunday, the first consignment of offshore maize bought last year by the Western Cape Maize Buyers Association.

A spokesman for the association confirmed that the maize formed part of the 230,000 tonnes it had bought from the U.S. and Argentina last year following concerns that South Africa could face a shortage.
Port authorities said the maize was loaded on the breakbulk vessel Athiniotissa and would take about two weeks to offload.
The association's spokesman said 70,000 tonnes of U.S. maize had been bought for delivery between January and March and a second ship would arrive in March carrying the rest of this tonnage.
Between April and July another four shipments of 40,000 tonnes a month would arrive from Argentina, the spokesman said.
"Altogether we have imported about 220,000-230,000 tonnes of maize," he said.

The association began contracting for imports last September amid fears that South Africa could face a yellow maize shortage of up to 700,000 tonnes after domestic supplies were drained by a high level of exports and deliveries to the Maize Board's export pools.
This was despite an expected bumper crop of 9.484 million tonnes, more than double the 4.406 million of 1995.
The shortage was more acute in coastal areas such as the Western Cape province which are furthest from the central maize-growing belt.

The Maize Board, however, said in October it expected the country to have a shortfall of only 154,000 tonnes of yellow maize and a surplus of 584,000 tonnes of white maize at the end of the current season on April 30.
The association said maize would be imported beyond the start of the new season in view of calls by the National Maize Producers' Organisation that farmers scale down their plantings.
